chantedPrayers.text:
LIBERATING PRAYER

O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha,
Precious treasury of compassion,
Bestower of supreme inner peace,
You, who love all beings without exception,
Are the source of happiness and goodness;
And you guide us to the liberating path.

Your body is a wishfulfilling jewel,
Your speech is supreme, purifying nectar,
And your mind is refuge for all living beings.

With folded hands I turn to you,
Supreme unchanging friend,
I request from the depths of my heart:

Please give me the light of your wisdom
To dispel the darkness of my mind
And to heal my mental continuum.

Please nourish me with your goodness,
That I in turn may nourish all beings
With an unceasing banquet of delight.

Through your compassionate intention,
Your blessings and virtuous deeds,
And my strong wish to rely upon you,
May all suffering quickly cease
And all happiness and joy be fulfilled;
And may holy Dharma flourish for evermore.

GOING FOR REFUGE

I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment,
Go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma and Sangha. (3x)

GENERATING BODHICHITTA

Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections,
May I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. (3x)

GENERATING THE FOUR IMMEASURABLES

May everyone be happy,
May everyone be free from misery,
May no one ever be separated from their happiness,
May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment.

VISUALIZING THE FIELD FOR ACCUMULATING MERIT

In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars.

PRAYER OF SEVEN LIMBS

With my body, speech and mind, humbly I prostrate,
And make offerings both set out and imagined.
I confess my wrong deeds from all time,
And rejoice in the virtues of all.
Please stay until samsara ceases,
And turn the Wheel of Dharma for us.
I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment.

OFFERING THE MANDALA

The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers,
The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon,
Seen as a Buddha Land and offered thus,
May all beings enjoy such Pure Lands.

I offer without any sense of loss
The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred and confusion,
My friends, enemies and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments;
Please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons.

IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI

PRAYER OF THE STAGES OF THE PATH

The path begins with strong reliance
On my kind Teacher, source of all good;
O Bless me with this understanding
To follow him with great devotion.

This human life with all its freedoms,
Extremely rare, with so much meaning;
O Bless me with this understanding
All day and night to seize its essence.

My body, like a water bubble,
Decays and dies so very quickly;
After death come results of karma,
Just like the shadow of a body.

With this firm knowledge and remembrance
Bless me to be extremely cautious,
Always avoiding harmful actions
And gathering abundant virtue.

Samsara's pleasures are deceptive,
Give no contentment, only torment;
So please bless me to strive sincerely
To gain the bliss of perfect freedom.

O Bless me so that from this pure thought
Come mindfulness and greatest caution,
To keep as my essential practice
The doctrine's root, the Pratimoksha.

Just like myself all my kind mothers
Are drowning in samsara's ocean;
O So that I may soon release them,
Bless me to train in bodhichitta.

But I cannot become a Buddha
By this alone without three ethics;
So bless me with the strength to practice
The Bodhisattva's ordination.

By pacifying my distractions
And analyzing perfect meanings,
Bless me to quickly gain the union
Of special insight and quiescence.

When I become a pure container
Through common paths, bless me to enter
The essence practice of good fortune,
The supreme vehicle, Vajrayana.

The two attainments both depend on
My sacred vows and my commitments;
Bless me to understand this clearly
And keep them at the cost of my life.

By constant practice in four sessions,
The way explained by holy Teachers,
O Bless me to gain both the stages,
Which are the essence of the Tantras.

May those who guide me on the good path,
And my companions all have long lives;
Bless me to pacify completely
All obstacles, outer and inner.

May I always find perfect Teachers,
And take delight in holy Dharma,
Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly,
And gain the state of Vajradhara.

RECEIVING BLESSINGS AND PURIFYING

From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
The purpose of this meditation is to encourage and inspire us to generate bodhichitta. Because it allows us to relieve others of their suffering. We can remember that.

First of all, bodhichitta is like supreme nectar that is able to overcome the great power of death. It destroys the suffering of death by leading all sentient beings to the eternal, unsurpassable state of complete Buddhahood. Bodhichitta is also like an inexhaustible treasury that eliminates the poverty of all sentient beings by satisfying all their wishes.

How do Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, those supreme beings who possess bodhichitta, eliminate poverty? By providing us with inexhaustible Dharma teachings and material gifts that can temporarily fulfill our spiritual and physical needs. Furthermore, by leading us to the everlasting state of happiness and complete enlightenment, they can ultimately free us from all poverty. It is in this respect that bodhichitta is like an inexhaustible treasury.

Bodhichitta is like supreme medicine that can relieve the mental and physical sickness of all sentient beings. Once we've taken the medicine of bodhichitta, we will gradually be cured of all diseases of body and mind. With his or her mind continuously filled with the medicine of bodhichitta, a bodhisattva is immune to suffering.

Just as a shady tree provides refreshment for a tired traveler, bodhichitta provides shade and rest for the exhausted sentient beings wandering along the paths of samsara. And finally, bodhichitta is like a universal bridge that leads beings from the suffering of the lower realms to the happiness of the higher realms and ultimately to Buddhahood. In our meditation, we contemplate how bodhichitta benefits other people like nectar, an inexhaustible treasury, a supreme medicine, a celestial shady tree, and a universal bridge.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text: You can just really admire bodhichitta through contemplating any or all of these analogies. Through contemplating in this way, if a strong determination arises to generate bodhichitta, you can just hold that in our heart, single-pointedly, as our object of meditation. If we become distracted, we then return to really admiring bodhichitta and how it relieves others of their suffering by comparing it to nectar, an inexhaustible treasury, a supreme medicine, a celestial shady tree, and a universal bridge.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text: We really admire these benefits and, again, transform our mind into the object of meditation, a strong wish to develop bodhichitta so that we can relieve others of their suffering. And then, we can just rejoice in our effort, thinking how wonderful it is to put some energy into meditating today. You can think, may this practice be the greatest benefit to all living beings.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text: And in our own time, we can gradually rise from our practice. Welcome back, everyone. Thanks so much for being here on this rainy day. Nice job not melting on your way. Well, H2O never hurt anyone, except for little cute sugar cubes and rain-averse people.

postMeditation.speaker: David
postMeditation.text: Anyone want to be our reader for today?

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text: Or cantor for today? Alexis, yep, thanks. Head cantor. Oh, yeah, sorry, the numbers. It will be 28 to 34, please.

shantidevaReading.text:
(28) Just as it is rare indeed
For a blind person to find a jewel in a heap of rubbish,
So too, by some very rare chance,
I have generated bodhichitta.

(29) It is the supreme nectar that overcomes
The dominion of death over living beings,
And an inexhaustible treasury
That dispels all their poverty.

(30) It is the supreme medicine that relieves
The sickness of living beings,
And a shady tree that provides shelter
For weary beings travelling samsara's paths.

(31) It is a universal bridge by which all living beings
Can be delivered from the lower realms,
And a rising moon of a mind
That relieves the torment of their delusions.

(32) It is a vast sun that completely dispels
The fog of unknowing from living beings.
It is the quintessential butter that arises
When the milk of Dharma is churned.

(33) For the honoured guests, the beings on samsara's paths
Who wish to enjoy the delights of bliss,
Bodhichitta will satisfy them all
By leading them to the supreme state of bliss.

(34) Today, in the presence of all the Protectors,
I invite all living beings to be my guests
To enjoy these temporary and ultimate delights.
May gods, demi-gods and everyone else be joyful!

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text: Thank you very much. Okay, so we're up to all sorts of fun stuff over the week, working with our delusions in general. And then we were also, we looked at meditation a bit — purpose, object, actual meditation. Oh my gosh, too much stuff. We'll keep it simpler today. Transforming adversity and all sorts of other weird and wonderful things. No, not weird, just wonderful things. Okay, anyone have anything they'd like to report from the field, from your practice over this last week? Fran, yes, thank you.

practiceReports.speaker: Fran
practiceReports.text: So this time I didn't have to write it down because it's pretty straightforward. So my practice is more of what I didn't do than what I did do. The last time I reported how it went so well with dedicating to destroy my distraction, and how I had this upward cycle of dedicating and then doing, practicing moral discipline and dedicating more, and it just was an upward cycle and everything was great. Until I stopped — it started to wane, the dedications. And I quickly noticed how when I stopped doing it, I stopped doing it. It caused me to stop doing it. And my whole mood changed, and what was delightful two weeks ago was now — being a Buddhist is too hard. It's so hard. There's just so much going on here, so much responsibility. And so it was definitely an exercise in doing it, it causes doing it, and not doing it causes not doing it.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: It's going in and out. Is there another mic in there? It might just be running out of battery.

practiceReports.speaker: Fran
practiceReports.text: Yeah, it is.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Okay.

practiceReports.speaker: Fran
practiceReports.text: It was an exercise in doing it creates doing it and not doing it creates not doing it. And I can notice the difference in my mood and my rejoicing in my practice — came in here today really sort of grumbly. And I had a conversation with James who related to me how something that Ryan related to him when he was questioning about not being happy about volunteering. And the answer was that you're not delighting in virtue. And that quickly turned me around because that's exactly what I needed to hear and it changed the whole thing. So my practice this coming week will be to start dedicating again.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Great. Thanks, Fran. Yeah, it's a helpful point about the momentum. As you said, doing it kind of leads to more doing it and not doing it leads to more not doing it. And it's very helpful to understand that every action that we perform also reinforces a behavior. So we have to really internalize that — it is a very powerful moment. It's part of understanding karma, right? But every action isn't just a one-off action. Every action reinforces a behavior and creates a momentum to go towards that behavior even more. So the more we reinforce it really makes us mindful and thoughtful about what we kind of say, think, do. Because we sort of realize, oh, it's not just — I'm not doing this practice today, or I'm just going to distract myself a little bit or follow this anger. It's not just doing that, right? I am reinforcing this behavior to repeatedly happen. And we have to really sit with that idea and have it touch our heart. It's related a bit to there being a karmic effect of tendency similar to the cause. That's the reinforcement, but it's also related to the idea that karma increases. Every karmic action we perform then increases the momentum. So it's not like a linear kind of relationship, right? Anyway, yeah, I think it's a really helpful insight and we're just like, oh, okay. I'm not going to get down on myself about it, but I'm going to remember that there's this momentum from both the positive side, which is really encouraging, but also the negative side, which is a little spooky and it gives us a little pause, maybe. Let me start feeding it. Thanks so much, Fran. Nice that the words of friends also came in handy. Marianne? Yep. And then Anne and then Suzanne.

practiceReports.speaker: Marianne
practiceReports.text: Hi, everybody at home. Yeah, I'm working with subtle impermanence. I hope it's in the curriculum.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Always. Yeah, sure.

practiceReports.speaker: Marianne
practiceReports.text: Because a while ago I was thinking about things coming and rising, going down, appearing, and then coming again fresh every moment. And then I just decided that instead of being ready or in a bad mood or worried about some samsaric stuff — like what to do that day, responsibilities — I just decided I was going to go out and meet that halfway and watch how I'm integrating with what's happening, how I'm influencing what's happening just by being more active and just going, I'm going to meet whatever's happening, kind of like meeting it halfway. I know it's hard to describe.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, I don't understand yet, but I really do want to understand. Why don't you give an example?

practiceReports.speaker: Marianne
practiceReports.text: Just like if you had to talk to someone, you're worried about the conversation. If I just push up my energy, put some energy in there and just go out and meet it, meet the situation with a positive mind, I can notice right away it's not what I thought it was going to be. It's something very much better. And then I know also it's because it's just the net of cause and effect. There was nothing really to stop me from doing that. There's something real about it. It's just that the whole world is impermanent. So it's very easy to influence.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: No, that makes sense. Okay, now it makes sense. I got you. Yeah, it's a kind of nice thing to play around with, especially if we're in a fearful state or a paralyzed state where we're stuck. And in these moments, we're kind of forgetting that acting changes the whole dynamic, right? Just by perceiving it, acting on a situation, it changes it. So if we're sitting on a sideline stuck and paralyzed, metaphorically speaking, and we're like, it's not changing, it's not looking different — basically, we're trying to make it this permanent, inherent thing. It's the situation, right? And we're not realizing, it's actually acting on it, moving towards it, changing our perception of it — that actually will change that situation itself, right? And so the kind of paralyzed and stuck mind is really relating to things in a very fixed, inherent way. And it's not realizing, oh, I'm influencing this. It's influenceable. It's changeable. It's completely malleable. Just by moving towards it and thinking about it and engaging with it, it's going to shift, right? So I think that's what you're saying, right?

practiceReports.speaker: Marianne
practiceReports.text: That's exactly it. Yeah, he nailed it.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah. And it's a really nice kind of thing to play around with. It's a big lie that the fearful mind plays on us, right? Always wants us to duck out and run away and not engage. And it's actually kind of a very prideful mind because it assumes it knows everything. It's like, granted, I know exactly how it's going to go. I'm not going to do it. There's a lot of pride in that thought, right? How do you know? You have no idea how it's going to go. So all it does is reinforce that stuck state. Yeah, so we do need a lot of courage. Anyway, yeah, just by acting, it changes, right? Some sort of quantum physics thing there, too. Just by engaging with it, it changes. It's just the very fact that we're engaging with it — it's morphing and adjusting and rearranging.

practiceReports.speaker: Marianne
practiceReports.text: Thank you for saying that in an articulate way.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, I gotcha. Thanks for sharing, Marianne. Anne, I think you're next, and then Suzanne after that.

practiceReports.speaker: Anne
practiceReports.text: I'll make this really quick. I've been hitting concentration super hard. Both sitting practice and all day long. And I was feeling a little grouchy about it because it seemed like it was very difficult to sustain the effort. It's like, I can do it, but it's like holding a bowling ball over your head, you know? Anyway, the first thing that was helpful is I have a friend. He's kind of in a different tradition, but we talk about Dharma a lot. And I complained to him. That was helpful. But he's just like, why are you trying to do this all by yourself? And he reminded me that I can ask for help. So going forward, instead of trying to use my ordinary mind, which delights in distraction, to try to tame my ordinary mind, I just started asking for help from the Buddhas. Help me concentrate. And the more I'm saying it, I'm like, wow, that's really smart. Now I just want to do it more. Just like every time I'm trying to do my meditation break practice, or I get distracted while I meditate, it's just an opportunity to ask for help. My ordinary mind, if I just try to use it to improve, I'm going to make such incremental progress, I'm going to die trying, you know? But if I have help from the Buddhas, if I keep relying on them more and more and more, I'm going to be really good.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, gotcha. That's really nice. It's good advice from the friend. Yeah, we always need to come back to things like the five forces, right, which show us how we actually change. And just meditating is the force of familiarity, right? Motivation is one force that's basically growing our faith in the thing that we're interested in, like in concentration in this case, and wishing for it. But then there's accumulating merit, purifying negativity, receiving blessings. So these five together function to make personal change. So often what happens is we get stuck in one little node, right? And some people, the issue is the meditation bit — they're missing that bit, and they need to put in that time. But sometimes it's something else. Oh, I'm not in the purification bit, I'm not in the blessings bit. And it's a nice kind of reminder to zoom out sometimes, like if we're deep into one, and we're not getting that movement anymore, the traction isn't there. It's like, okay, let me step back, let me look at the five forces. Which one is missing, or which ones are missing? And often, if we just nurture one or the other, we'll get some movement again, and then we're back into action. So in this case, it's the blessings bit — asking for help. It's just a great meditation tool to remember this, anytime we're struggling with something. Okay, zoom out, which one's missing? It's usually a couple raising their hand, eagerly begging us to go towards them. And we're like, oops, okay, we do that, and all of a sudden it's easy again, it's nice, it's joyful. Thanks so much, Anne. Great point. Suzanne, yes?

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: Hi, everyone. So over the last week, over the last few weeks, I've noticed my health getting a little worse, and especially the last week, Monday, I really crashed. And I'm finding myself leaning into the patient acceptance. I'm thinking I did pretty much everything I wanted this summer, and it wore me out. And it's okay. I could rest now, and it's fine. Yeah, I think this time of year is just really hard for me. The days get shorter, going into winter, even though the fall's kind of nice. I just have a very hard time, almost every year I think I noticed it, but I think it's a little seasonal affective disorder, but it seems to level out when winter comes and I'm used to the whole thing for some reason. I don't know why, it's very odd. Anyway, the only day I went out was on Thursday. And it was wishing love day. And I was sending everybody love as I passed them on the street. And kind of weird things happened. I mean, I felt very good, like in my mind, I felt very loving towards the people, and they started coming up on the street and talking to me, which is very unusual. And I find it kind of easy to practice when I'm out and about, but if I'm going to be home, which I was for most of the week, I find it not as easy. I know it should be all equal and emptiness, but I'm not quite there yet. I'm just wondering if there's any tips that you could give me to practice more. I mean, I guess, if I get a text or a phone call, I could concentrate on that person. Other than that, any other ideas to keep it fresh and moving along?

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, thanks, Suzanne. Do you, in your day, let's say you're going to have a lot of time at home in that day — do you have a schedule?

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: I do, I have a bunch of things I want to do, whether I get to them, it depends. Sometimes, like, I've been trying to get to cleaning my shower all week, and I just don't have the energy to do it. So I've been doing other things I don't want to do instead that take less energy. But, and then I have, I often have class, either yoga or meditation class. I mean, yesterday, it was all day of workshops.

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: I have another question about that also. But let's —

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, let's stick with this, though. So I think what you're bringing up is a really important point. And it's important for all of us in our own way. Because you're noticing, okay, when I was out and about, I was connecting to this wishing love feeling and then I'm home, then it's not exactly grooving and so on. And the thing here is there's a tyranny of structurelessness. Basically, when things are completely structureless, there's a tyranny that happens. And it's coming from mostly self-cherishing, because it happens when there's no structure in the day. I'm not saying this is exactly your case, but it's just a point that will be generally useful for all of us. When there's no structure in the day, then what happens is that our mind just keeps defaulting to the loudest voice in the mind, to choose what we do next. And generally speaking, for most ordinary people, the self-cherishing mind is the loudest voice in the mind. And so basically what happens is that the self-cherishing mind keeps deciding what to do all day. Let's do this now. Let's do that now. And there is a tyranny there. There's a domination that happens. It's similar to in a lawless society or situation, some big, dumb, brutal, vicious being rises to the top, at least in the short run, because they're the one willing to beat up everyone and take power and take control. And they're not very reasonable. And so the delusions, especially the big, dumb, brutal, violent delusions, like self-cherishing, usually take charge when there's no structure. And so in some of our cases, we might spend a lot of time at home, maybe it's because of a job situation or retirement or health or not having all the connections or whatever. And so when we're at home, it becomes a structureless environment. And it's very easy then for the big, dumb, evil delusions to take charge and just control everything — basically they start to just choose what we do. And so in those cases, we need to make a plan for ourselves. The plan might be from four to five-thirty, do whatever you want and have some fun, but it's still part of a plan. It's part of a structure. And then from five-thirty to seven or whatever — okay, yeah, maybe we want to read some book or lay on the couch, but it's still part of a structure. It's not just randomly, now I'm reading a book and laying on the couch. It was part of the plan. And every day, if this is our kind of life cycle, we should do that either the night before for the next day or first thing in the morning. And we plan out the day and it has the different themes. You have some fun things in there, some silly things — it could be totally meaningless things, really meaningful spiritual things, selfless things, going out, whatever. But it has to have some kind of scaffolding like this, or else what's going to happen — our days are going to blend together. Weeks are going to blend together. Months are going to blend together. Years are going to blend together. And our life is going to disappear. And the one thing that grew in strength through that chaos — the delusions — that's what ends up happening. Yeah, so this is an idea — Suzanne, I think what you'll find is that will really help the meditation practice. Every day, even if I'm not going out much today, I'm still having a plan. And the plan, again, could have flexibility within the things that I plan, but it's still on the schedule. And I think you'll find that this is really helpful. It kind of contains the mental energy. It also feels really good. It makes the day really intentional. It doesn't let the self-cherishing mind dominate the flow in the day. And we might have to do a few iterations where we kind of try and it doesn't exactly happen. But then the day will actually start to feel very rich and we'll get a lot done that we need to get done. We'll do the chores we need to do, but we'll also do the kind of spiritual things we need to do. And actually, we'll probably have more fun doing the fun things that we do, because they'll just sort of be part of a very sensible, thoughtful structure in the day. So I hope that speaks to what you're talking about, but I think this would be a really nice idea.

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: I do think I have a schedule in my head of things I want to do, but the delusions come in and that's when I pick up the phone. Yeah, it's all connecting now. And when you were saying the days and months are rolling into each other, I totally feel that. And life is slipping away and the time is passing. Yeah, all that.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, yeah. And it's really like the schedule in the head isn't the same as the schedule on some paper or on the computer or something. It's just not the same.

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: I need Anne's schedule.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah. Anne over and she can schedule it all.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, a little spiritual scheduling is a really nice thing to do. And it's important — if you think about the monasteries, right? The monasteries from one point of view are like these structureless environments. These people are on retreat just hanging out. But it's not at all. It's really like 6 to 7, this. 7 to 7:30, this. 7:30 to 9:30, this.

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: Yeah, I feel like that's too much though.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, it doesn't need to be too rigid, but it's really worth it to write it down and to make it every day.

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: I will try that. Can I ask you a quick question regarding just practice in general — when you're on retreat or have a day like yesterday where you're doing a lot of hours of listening to Dharma. I'm having trouble fitting in the six sessions when I'm doing that. I mean, what do you do? I'm just throwing it out there.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, I mean, we just do our best really. If you went to everything we did yesterday, we had four different teachings, right? So yeah, you can think of them a little bit like your sessions. The six sessions as normal might not be perfectly around that. That's okay. We're just doing our best here. To me, if I really go to a Dharma class with all my heart and really try to focus and practice and engage with it, it is so obviously spiritually beneficial. It's definitely in line with the idea behind the six sessions. So anyway, I think the main thing there is just we just do our best and we really celebrate our wins on those days. Okay. Other people — Ryan and then Mimi, please.

practiceReports.speaker: Ryan
practiceReports.text: Two things I noticed this week. One of them is, you said in the GP class last Sunday, and I remember very clearly. And I quote: where there is unhappiness, there is attachment. Simple as that. And whenever I remembered, of course, when I remembered and I watched and I noticed unhappiness, yes, there was attachment, including yesterday without going into the stories. So that's number one. Number two, talking about structurelessness, going back to what you said — I can write a book about that. But I would say is that I followed the lamrim wagon the last month, since the No-D celebration. And I think you noticed that when I was talking about it — you mentioned you were like, you're throwing a line when I was complaining about where's the joy in the volunteering. I think that should be a hint. I mean, yes, I find the purpose, but where is the joy?

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Keep it on. It's lamrim.

practiceReports.speaker: Ryan
practiceReports.text: And you said, okay, Ryan, where's the unhappiness there? And then it started to hit me this week. Oh, yes. Because I followed them. This is another sign. Whenever there is no lamrim around in life, there is no happiness. What was I thinking? Because I took on all the different projects. It's very important for me to make sure the apartment's clean and other things. Everything has to smell good, my laundry and other things. And other things that are more important to me that I get restless if it's not — little dust or whatever, but there's dust in my mind, irritation that doesn't add to me. And especially talking about structures.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Please reach a conclusion.

practiceReports.speaker: Ryan
practiceReports.text: So a conclusion is, especially with all these hours, and I can agree with you that days and weeks and months go by and just blend. And without lamrim — yeah, there's no happiness, and it blends.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, thanks, Ryan. I think that makes sense. And I think you found the culprit. Both those are related points — where there is unhappiness, there's attachment, hundred percent of the time. And then why is there unhappiness and attachment? Well, lamrim practice got thrown to the curb. Especially when we're in a bit of a structure that's appeared in our life, a spiritual structure like that is a lifesaver. I mean, even if the rest of the day isn't structured, at least that is there as a backbone every day to give a theme to the day, a spiritual message to the day. At least that, right? We don't want a day where there's not some kind of spiritual lens to look at the day with — that's a dead day, a dead empty day. So, yeah, this will happen, right? We kind of go on and off the wagon with things like lamrim. But I think once we start to notice the pattern of the benefit it brings, sometimes by moving away from it, then at some point it will click — this is part of my life. And this is how I want my life to be. Anyway, thanks, Ryan. I appreciate you sharing that.

practiceReports.speaker: Mimi
practiceReports.text: I'm targeting attachment for a companion. And also writing a reflection. So this week, I was on target. And I did my six sessions. And one of the things that I noticed — I noticed a couple of things, I'll keep it succinct. Sounds really mundane, but something happened. Because I had this thought — this really, it's not a realization — I've had this thought or awareness that what has kept me in samsara, round and round and round again, is my attachment to my desires. Attachment. That is the reason why I haven't gotten out and become enlightened. And I don't know, I mean, I hear it all the time. But something — it went inside. And then I thought about this, that this attachment is like an addiction. It's like a mind that keeps lurching out. And it's like an addict. And I'm totally repulsed by it. And then you said in the teaching yesterday, that really resonated with me — you said, you have to come to the depth of your awareness or something like that, regarding this hallucination. And I was like, yeah, this is a hallucination. And I have to get in there. Yeah, that's what I've been working on.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, lovely. It's a great point that you're raising. And yeah, of course, we know it intellectually. Okay, it's my attachment, it's keeping me stuck. But it's different than getting a beautiful spiritual experience of that recognition. And that sounds like what you're connecting to. There's one of these little famous lines that are just so rich and amazing — I think it's in How to Understand the Mind. Let me see if I got it nearby. It's in the attachment section. Yeah, so here it is. This is a whole dependent relationship. It's page 116. So it says here: what are the faults of attachment? In the sutras, Buddha says that living beings are bound within the prison of samsara by the rope of desire's attachment. And then here's the dependent relationship. The reason we experience suffering and problems is that we remain in samsara. The reason we remain in samsara is that we have made no effort to escape. The reason we have made no effort to escape is that we have no wish to escape. And the reason we have no wish to escape is that we are so strongly attached to the places, enjoyments, and bodies of samsara. Therefore attachment is the root of all our suffering and problems. It's a lovely thing to meditate on, and it actually breaks down the whole cycle. And the whole dependent relationship is drawn out, and each one can be its own little contemplation. So the reason we experience suffering and problems is that we remain in samsara, period. There's no other reason — it's that we're in samsara. All problems and suffering can be blamed on samsara. Not people, not this, not that — just samsara. Then, the reason we remain in samsara is that we've made no effort to escape. So let me meditate on that — I've made no effort, actually, to escape. And then the third: the reason we have made no effort to escape is that we have no wish to escape. Of course, from wish comes effort, right? So, oh, I have no wish, relative to our wish to enjoy the things of samsara. We don't have much of a wish, at least most people. So what would it take to have a greater wish? And then finally, why don't we have that wish? The reason we have no wish to escape is that we're so strongly attached to the places, enjoyments, and bodies of samsara. So it's those things that are drawn out specifically — places, enjoyments, and bodies of samsara, both our own and others' bodies. Yeah, so it's inviting us — okay, well, then where do we want to work on in this dependent relationship? It's probably somewhere around there, right? Let me start breaking down that attachment. It's interesting too — in highest yoga tantra practice, you talk about the four complete purities: bodies, environment, enjoyments, and activities. And they're a bit alluded to here — it's the attachment towards those things that bind us in samsara. So if we want to purify, it's by practicing tantra that we can purify those things, and therefore purify the attachment, and then leave samsara. Okay, anyway, that's enough for now. Okay, thanks everyone. That's lovely.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Thank you for the juicy, delightful data. So now, back to the text — Meaningful to Behold, full acceptance of bodhichitta, page 141, bestowing great benefit and happiness upon others. Bodhichitta is like a host who invites sentient beings as his or her guests to a banquet of higher rebirth, liberation, and the unsurpassable delight of enlightenment. By the power of his bodhichitta, a bodhisattva brings others to the state of happiness and complete fulfillment. All living beings are wandering, lost in the desert of samsara and thirsting for happiness. Who is able to lead them from this wilderness? The one who possesses the precious mind of bodhichitta. Exhorting others to meditate on happiness — Shantideva summarizes the third concluding activity that seals our full acceptance of bodhichitta as follows: today, in the presence of the protectors, I invite all sentient beings to a banquet of unsurpassable delight. Let all those who appreciate Dharma, you gods, demigods, nagas, and humans, rejoice and be happy.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: So far, Shantideva has given extensive explanations of various Dharma methods, but how do we actually put them into practice? We do this by means of analytical and placement meditation on the teachings we have received. First, we must take a critical look at each subject, trying to understand its meaning and relevance for our lives. Judging, testing, and trying to understand the teachings in this way is called analytical meditation. Once we've done this, and come to some conclusion concerning the object of meditation, we should place our mind upon it single-pointedly. This is known as placement or formal meditation. If we think that meditation means sitting with an empty mind, we will receive no benefit, no matter how long we meditate. The object of meditation can be a particular aspect of the teaching, such as the benefits of bodhichitta, or the form of a personal deity, or even our breath. Whatever object we choose, we should examine it fully to gain a clear idea of it. For example, in order to develop single-pointed concentration, we can meditate on a visualized figure of a Buddha, choosing such a figure because it represents all the wisdom and methods of the path. We begin by selecting a painting or statue that represents such a figure clearly. We should examine this image minutely, scrutinizing it from the crown of its head to its feet and back to the crown again. By doing this well, we will gain a rough mental image of a Buddha's body. This then becomes our object to visualize in meditation. When we sit quietly and try to see this image in our mind's eye, holding the object with mindfulness and checking with alertness, we will be engaged in placement meditation.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: This entire process can be likened to setting out on a journey. If we wish to go to London, we must first gain an accurate understanding of which road to take. Otherwise, we might arrive in Manchester, which is very disappointing. In a similar fashion, if we want to engage in placement meditation and dwell upon an object single-pointedly, we must gain a thorough understanding of that object by means of analytical meditation. Otherwise, our efforts will be wasted and many faults will arise. This point cannot be overstated. It is a big mistake to try to meditate on nothing. If we have a proper object in meditation, there is the possibility that we can progress along the nine levels of concentration and achieve the single-pointed concentration of tranquil abiding, Sanskrit shamatha. Without a proper object of meditation, there will be little to show from even a thousand years of sitting. Everything that has been explained so far in this commentary and everything that is to follow are objects for meditation. There's not a single teaching in Shantideva's text that is not to be meditated on. Thus, it is very important to learn the art of meditation correctly and to be able to apply it in our everyday life.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Okay, so there's a lot here. Let's start back with structure. In Clear Light of Bliss, there's this amazing bit on the section of tranquil abiding where Geshe-la says, to train in concentration, one good idea would be to divide every meditation into eighteen subsections. So a specific eighteen. And the idea is you do eighteen rounds of analytical and placement meditation shots, and then you're done. It's like, okay, let me try to find the object of meditation through some analysis. Okay, I've got some kind of gist. Oh, I'm distracted. That's subsection one, done. Then, okay, let me try again. Oh, distracted within one second. That's subsection two, done. Like that. Until eighteen, and then you're done. Just take a break. It might be two minutes, or if the subsections are really small, it might be five minutes, or twenty minutes. I'm not suggesting that we be as specific as that, but there's something very beautiful to meditation that's like that, because what happens is our mind starts to train in high-quality meditation. And our mind is pattern-based — it just follows patterns. And so if we have a pattern of meditating very sloppily, that pattern then replicates. If we meditate in a very sloppy way, it reinforces the habit to then meditate in a sloppy way the next time. So from one point of view, trying is succeeding, right? Trying versus not trying is still way better because at least we're reinforcing the fact that we're trying. But then once we start trying, it's nice to think, okay, do I have some bad habits in meditation? Once I'm on the cushion, do I have some wandering, undisciplined mental habits that I kind of feed? And if so, can I start to tighten up the ship a little bit and approach it a bit more systematically, in a more structured way?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: On our tranquil abiding retreat that we had a couple weeks ago, we were talking about this idea of creating an orderly mind, an organized mind. And this is what happens when we train in concentration in a systematic way. Our mind starts to become organized — it functions like a system, like a very clear, coherent system, not like a random chaotic mess. And so one of the ways to start to do that is whenever we meditate, to really try to create this discipline of analytical meditation, placement meditation, when we're distracted — with a very disciplined mind we stop. It is really useful then to pause a little bit and make sure all the distraction energy subsides. Sometimes breathing meditation or whatever else helps. And then once it's subsided, then back in — analytical meditation, placement meditation, distracted, stop. Not whip the mind back into the meditation, which ends up creating a very fuzzy, ambiguous mess of a meditation. We're trying to create an organized, structured meditation experience. Generally speaking, 10 minutes of a structured meditation is way more useful than 30 minutes of an unstructured meditation. Because the habit that's creating is one of organization, mental organization, mental discipline. And that ends up paying out in the long run. A 30-minute wandering meditation might end up reinforcing some pretty funky behavior — sometimes even discouragement, sometimes just following whatever comes to mind, brainstorming habits, stuff like that. And then it's stuff we have to unlearn, which is annoying. So this is Je Tsongkhapa's way of meditating. He's always there, but he really formalized the system and taught it very precisely — to always meditate like this and to really try to not make it a wandering, brainstorming session.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Okay, so that's just the first thing — let's approach our meditations like this. Structured. Analytical meditation towards an object of meditation that's clearly defined. We find it. We rest our mind there in concentration. We wander. Pause a bit. I was encouraging people to do about 10 rounds of breathing meditation at that point. That's what I do to get rid of that distracted energy. Once it really subsides, I don't need to. But if the mind's a bit busy, I often need to pause for about 10 breaths every single time I get distracted to kind of get to a more subtle place. Sometimes five is okay, but not many less for me. But anyway, then you may have a clear feeling — okay, I've put down the distraction energy. Now I'm back to analytical meditation. Thinking this, thinking that. Okay, placement meditation. Like that. So that's one thing about structured meditations. Eventually, it will evolve into seeking, finding, holding, remaining, which is the more elaborate version of it. But at first, it's great — if we don't have much of a structure, just keep it simple. Analytical, placement, distracted, stop. Put down all that restless, busy stuff. Quiet down. Analytical, placement, distracted, stop, pause. Start again.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Then, Geshe-la gives the example of meditating on a Buddha image. And in terms of concentration sutra, this is the object of meditation that Buddha encouraged people to try to train in concentration on. And Joyful Path, Geshe-la explains a bit about it there too. I'm not saying we should all go do this, but there are a few obvious advantages of a Buddha image. One is that it's just an image. And it's way easier to meditate on an image than a very complicated concept like bodhichitta or something like that. It's a huge, complex meditation to get to bodhichitta. There's so much in there. How do you actually train in concentration? I'm holding my love. I'm holding my compassion. I'm holding my exchanging self with others. I'm holding a wish to protect other people. I'm holding a concept of enlightenment. That's a lot for a mind to hold in a concentrated way. An image of a Buddha is just an image of a Buddha. That's literally what it is. A child can do that. So that's one reason that Buddha image meditation is so helpful. Second reason is because they're so pure, and we say they're outside samsara. And so whenever you meditate or look at a Buddha image, you're creating a pure uncontaminated karma. It doesn't even matter your motivation. It's creating a karma that is an indestructible imprint that will lead you out of samsara one day. It's one of the unique qualities of Buddha images. So whenever we meditate on a Buddha image, it's automatically creating this good effect. In addition, it's also very easy to tell whether our concentration has degraded or not. So it's easy to tell if we should oppose mental sinking or excitement, or tighten up our concentration or loosen it, because the image will start to fade, for example. Oh, that's mental sinking in action — I've got to tighten up my focus. Oh, I'm kind of moving on to other things. Oh, that's mental excitement. Oh, it's shaking a little bit — I'm a little too intense. That's subtle mental excitement. Oh, my grip is fading just very slightly. That's subtle mental sinking. So it's actually much easier to notice the flaws of concentration with an image, as opposed to something like patience towards someone who's harmed you. How can you tell mental sinking in that patience?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Lastly, it's just so nice to meditate on a Buddha image because it's a completely safe and gentle meditation to do. The peacefulness of Buddha and the acceptance of Buddha towards us and the love of Buddha towards us is just so comforting and easy. And there's no scorn or judgment. It's not a hard thing to do. It's really like being with a friend. Like, we know if something awful happened to us — we're totally betrayed by a very close person in life — there might be a friend we would go to specifically. Someone that we know we could just go to and they would just hold that space for us and just be with us. And they wouldn't want anything from us. They wouldn't want us to put on a good face. They wouldn't try to coach us out of any feeling we're having. They would just be with us. And we could just be with them. We could just cry a bunch or make a big mess of it. And they just wouldn't care. And they would just be there and they would just love us. And we would know that they're totally safe to go to. And Buddhas are like that, but even far greater. They already know the whole situation. They love us. The Buddhas love us knowing the mess in our mind and knowing everything that we've done and not done. And they totally believe in us. They're rooting us on. And they're so gentle. And they have this long-term vision. And they're not in a rush. They're willing to just go with us for the long haul. And they're willing for it to be a many-life journey, even if it's thousands of lives to enlightenment. They're really okay with that. So the point is, it's just such a safe and comforting meditation to have in our back pocket. And just a healing meditation to have. Specifically, I want to talk about Buddha Shakyamuni here. The exquisite peace of Buddha Shakyamuni is a very nice thing to always connect to. Buddha's peacefulness and tranquility. Buddha's power comes from his tranquility and peacefulness. And it's an immovable quality. As Geshe-la says, describing patience in the New Eight Steps, he says our patience will become as stable as a mountain and as calm as the depths of the ocean. These images are so beautiful. And that's like Buddha. Buddha's like that, from his peacefulness. It's just this incredible stability and tranquility. And elsewhere, in Bodhisattva Vow, Geshe-la explains that Buddha abides in the tranquil ocean of reality, and his peace eternally radiates as compassion, gradually drawing all living beings to the same state.

mainTeaching.speaker: Anne
mainTeaching.text: This is going back to the question of creating bad habits while meditating. I often meditate to help me fall asleep. And I'm wondering, am I creating causes to fall asleep when I meditate?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Yeah, there's something to think about here. And I don't think we want to make a rule or decree on something like this. But this is something that I've come to different conclusions on at different parts of my practice. And what I would say is there are some meditations that help us become a bit more subtle. That will aid our sleep, which we need. We need to go to sleep. It's not helpful to sit there ruminating. It's not good for our mental health, not good for our physical health. But there are meditations that really do help with that. Like the yoga of sleeping helps with that. But it doesn't need to be the elaborate yoga of sleeping with all the imagery. It could just be the yoga of sleeping according to completion stage where you dissolve your guru into your heart. Everything becomes union of bliss and emptiness and you just abide in that space in your heart. That's very powerful to go to sleep with. There's also a clarity of mind meditation, which is very suitable for sleep because it's part of the six stages of Mahamudra where you identify your subtle mind and very subtle mind. So that's really nice to go to sleep with. And even before we lay down, doing it for five or ten minutes before we go to bed will really help the sleep process. But we do want to think — if we're doing some meditation basically solely to bore ourselves to the point where we want to go to sleep, that's not ideal. So it's a little bit different than what I'm describing. Using those yoga of sleep related meditations to become more subtle so that we can go to sleep is a very specific intention, and Buddha taught that. But if it's like, I'm going to do this meditation or listen to some teaching because it's basically going to bore me to such a degree that I'll go to sleep, then that's not a good habit. It's the same as listening to a teaching when we're doing something in a very distracted way. It's one thing if we're really focusing while we're doing something, like if we're going for a walk, listening to a teaching, and we're really focusing — yeah, that's fine, it's transforming the walk. But if it's just a little bit in the background and we're not engaging with it at all, it's a bit like we're training in some kind of distraction. Again, I'm not trying to suggest some rule, but the precept behind that is a very sensible one, which is we're always training in some habit. What's the habit we want to train in? And what habit are we training in at any moment? Okay, that's that. Thanks.

mainTeaching.speaker: Ryan
mainTeaching.text: Maybe you talked about gazing in class before. I might have missed it, but can you talk a little bit about it since you talked about meditating on the image of Buddha Shakyamuni? When I'm gazing on the Buddha, besides the physical looking, what's the process of gazing? Am I thinking about something contemplative, or just looking at the physical picture?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Yeah, how to do the gazing practice. Level one is you're just looking. You're not thinking about much. That's fine. You can almost be a little bit blank. And it's especially a practice when we've got not much in the tank, or we're tired or worn out or really sick. This is a great backup practice. You just stare and just let whatever happen happen. But it's like, I've got nothing else — I'm just going to look at Buddha. And a lot of practitioners who are amazing, very inspiring practitioners will tell me — I've heard over the years from different people independently at different times — sometimes I'll just go stare at Buddha. And it's interesting at this point, I've heard from so many people I really admire as practitioners that they do this. There's something to the practice that's very profound. And they understand, okay, I don't have much in the tank sometimes, but I can do that definitely. So that's level one — you're literally staring. You're not trying to control it too much. You're just looking at Buddha. But then we can elaborate. You can look at the Buddha's different qualities and admire them and think about them, different traits. For example, Buddha touching the ground — the earth represents having conquered the Devaputra Maras. So you can think about that and his life story. We can think about Buddha's inner qualities — wisdom, compassion, spiritual power, omniscience. We can feel Buddha's love for us and feel Buddha's looking at us with love and compassion. We can develop gratitude, thinking how Buddha saved our life and changed our life and has been helping us for eons very patiently. So we can make it very elaborate or it can just be literally staring, and everyone in between. But it's nice to know we've got that in our back pocket for those kind of days. It doesn't have to just be on those days, but sometimes there are just some days where we're so sick, physically, we can't think, we can't even read a Dharma book, we can't listen to a teaching. We've got no energy at all. And that's a really good practice in those times. You just sit there on your bed and you've got Buddha right there, and you can just stare. And that's a perfect practice. It's complete. Yeah, when we're restless, a fantastic thing to do. The sensory grounding helps when you're really restless — having something with our senses to do. And Buddha is a perfect experience with the senses. Okay, this is enough for now, I think. Thanks for asking.

announcements.speaker: Kadam Kyle
announcements.text: Okay, lovely. Thank you all so much. Then we'll begin the conscientiousness chapter in the next class. Very exciting. I'm thinking about reinforcing behavior or not. We just talked about reinforcing. So I have a decision that I'm making that I've already made, but I'm remaking it — I'll make it out loud. I'm not going to go with yelling out in class, ever, ever. It doesn't enforce a good behavior, and it's disrespectful, both to everyone in the class, actually. So I'm not going to reinforce that behavior, ever. Unless there's a fire or something like that — then please yell out.

dedication.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dedication.text: So let's dedicate now, and we'll come back at 6:16. We can think: the virtues we've collected, practicing, meditating, discussing — may all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications.

chantedPrayers.text:
LIBERATING PRAYER

O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha,
Precious treasury of compassion,
Bestower of supreme inner peace,
You, who love all beings without exception,
Are the source of happiness and goodness;
And you guide us to the liberating path.

Your body is a wishfulfilling jewel,
Your speech is supreme, purifying nectar,
And your mind is refuge for all living beings.

With folded hands I turn to you,
Supreme unchanging friend,
I request from the depths of my heart:

Please give me the light of your wisdom
To dispel the darkness of my mind
And to heal my mental continuum.

Please nourish me with your goodness,
That I in turn may nourish all beings
With an unceasing banquet of delight.

Through your compassionate intention,
Your blessings and virtuous deeds,
And my strong wish to rely upon you,
May all suffering quickly cease
And all happiness and joy be fulfilled;
And may holy Dharma flourish for evermore.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Okay, welcome back, everyone. Glad that we can all be here. So the conclusion from the last little bit is, okay, let's look at our meditation practice and just see if we can refine it in some different ways. And then we didn't read the concluding sentence. This concludes full acceptance of bodhichitta, the third chapter of the text Meaningful to Behold, commentary to Shantideva's Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life. Conscientiousness, yay! This is just all about having a strong wish to overcome delusions, mostly, but also some of the little bits and pieces. How to practice the six perfections. Having discussed the benefits of the mind of enlightenment, how to purify the non-virtue preventing the development of this mind, and how to accept this mind fully, Shantideva is now ready to explain how we can keep our bodhichitta from degenerating and how we can increase it.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: To the practice of the six perfections. Thus, the remainder of the text is divided into the following four parts. Meditating on conscientiousness so that the bodhichitta practice and precepts do not degenerate. How to train in moral discipline by practicing mindfulness and alertness. Explanation of the four remaining perfections — patience, effort, concentration, and wisdom. Dedication in the practice of giving for the benefit of all beings. It's previously been explained how the practitioner generates the mind of bodhichitta and takes the bodhisattva vows, dedicating him or herself to attainment of full enlightenment for the sake of others. However, if a bodhisattva is careless with his three doors of body, speech, and mind, he'll be unable to follow the practices correctly or keep his vows purely. Therefore, in order to prevent the precious bodhichitta from degenerating, Shantideva teaches the method of conscientiousness.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Conscientiousness is a mental factor that is vigilant in preventing us from wandering towards delusions and being distracted by meaningless activities of body, speech, and mind. Its opposite is a careless attitude of recklessness or unconcern leading to deluded activity, the creation of negative karma, and the degeneration of our practice and precepts. Recklessness can manifest through any of our three doors. To be careless with our bodies is to engage in actions that are in conflict with Dharma. This includes such things as killing, stealing, engaging in sexual misconduct, letting yourself become intoxicated, becoming addicted to gambling, and other similarly deluded misdeeds. In terms of our speech, recklessness manifests as lying, divisive speech, hurtful speech, and idle chatter. Finally, recklessness of mind includes all deluded thoughts such as covetousness, malice, and wrong views. If we are conscientious about our behavior, our understandings and realizations will automatically increase, while the defilements of our three doors will decrease.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Conscientiousness is essential for our practice and moral discipline. Generally, when a conscientious person speaks, he is polite, saying things that will benefit others as well as himself, and communicating about Dharma matters. The reckless person, on the other hand, speaks under the influence of delusion. His behavior is impolite, and what he says invariably upsets others and himself as well. Being conscientious about our three doors is the way to ensure that our positive virtuous qualities, including whatever bodhichitta we have developed, are stabilized and abundantly increased. If we wish to practice Dharma well, we must develop conscientiousness. All Dharma communities have codes of discipline, and ask the people living there to refrain from certain actions, such as smoking, drinking, gambling, and fighting. So no underground poker rings here, everyone. What is the reason for this discipline? It is not to punish the practitioners, though it might appear this way to some. Rather, these rules are laid down in order to help people practice conscientiously. Spiritual guides continually remind us to abandon non-virtue and keep our mind from the influence of delusion. They do this so that our actions of body, speech, and mind will be pure, and we'll be able to gain the fruits of spiritual practice. Beautiful.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: A bunch of lovely points woven through this. So basically, there are two kinds of minds being juxtaposed. There is conscientiousness and recklessness, or non-conscientiousness. And conscientiousness is a mind that really values virtue, and is vigilant against wandering towards delusion. It's really like a general in the mind that is in charge of the whole show. Of all the mental factors, this one coordinates everything from one point of view. It's like saying, okay, virtues, you go. Delusions, get out of here. Mindfulness and alertness, you get rid of that delusion there. Wisdom, come on, cut through that ignorance. It's really a central quality that's almost like an organizing factor — a mental factor that everything is routed through, that we want to feed and support. When we first start coming to Dharma classes, we learn a lot about delusions and overcoming them, and training in virtues. But it's helpful to think, what's the mindset specifically that's being trained in whenever we do that? The principal one is conscientiousness, and then it manifests as training in the different virtues, or opposing the different delusions. But it really is the mind that makes us actually value those virtuous minds, and want to oppose the deluded ones. It's a beautiful quality. And we've all trained in it a ton, just by being Buddhists. We might not have the name for it, but we all have that quality to some degree because we want to train in virtue, we want to overcome delusion. But this chapter is about formalizing that focus and emphasis.

teaching.speaker: Byron
teaching.text: Is conscientiousness a synonym for sense of shame? And if not, could you clarify what the difference would be?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, is conscientiousness the same as sense of shame? No, those are two different states of mind. The word conscientious, in modern American vernacular, can be kind of synonymous with something like sense of shame. I'm very conscientious, so I keep an eye on my behavior. But the meaning in Buddhist practice is a little bit different. I'll just read out the definitions. Sense of shame is a mind that avoids non-virtuous action out of consideration for oneself. Consideration for others is a mind that avoids non-virtuous actions out of care for others. So they're two sides of the same coin. One is practicing moral discipline and appropriate behavior for one's sake, and one is practicing appropriate behavior for the sake of others. Conscientiousness will help those two, but it's a slightly different emphasis. It's a bigger mind with a bit more going on. Geshe-la says here, page 86, How to Understand the Mind: the definition of conscientiousness is a mental factor that, in dependence upon effort, cherishes what is virtuous and guards the mind from delusion and non-virtue. So of course, that's going to help our sense of shame. It's going to help our consideration for others. But this is mostly about specifically being really interested in growing our virtues and abandoning our delusions. That's what conscientiousness is really focused on. Sense of shame is more about avoiding inappropriate actions out of concern for oneself. Or avoiding inappropriate actions for the sake of others, in the case of consideration. They're a little bit different. Does that make sense, Byron?

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: Thank you so much.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, thank you. Jose, yeah? Has anyone got the mic there?

teaching.speaker: Jose
teaching.text: I have a similar question, but first just a comment that I think is actually very interesting on this point. The delusion that I chose to practice with was non-conscientiousness. I haven't made much progress, to be honest. That's why I haven't really reported.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: You've been non-conscientious about dealing with non-conscientiousness.

teaching.speaker: Jose
teaching.text: But what I did do was read about it, and the definition is actually complex, so I went to the Spanish version of How to Understand the Mind. It's very interesting that the definition in Spanish, when you translate it word by word, would be like good behavior, or more like correct behavior — subrecta conducta. And that was very interesting for me. Conscientiousness is a word that is very hard to translate, and when you put it as good behavior, it's kind of completely different. And non-conscientiousness is bad behavior, basically. So that was just something interesting. But my question is, what's the difference between conscientiousness and moral discipline? Because those things kind of feel like the same. I think there's something that I'm missing there.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, what's the difference between conscientiousness and moral discipline? There's a lot of overlap, and one of the guiding factors in our moral discipline is our conscientiousness. It's part of the retinue of moral discipline. So the way that I think about it is that moral discipline is focused on the actions, and conscientiousness is focused on the minds that either lead to or don't lead to the actions. So they're very related. But in moral discipline, we often talk about engaging in virtuous actions, avoiding non-virtuous or inappropriate actions, engaging in actions that benefit others. It's really the law of karma — I want to engage in actions going in this direction. Conscientiousness is more the mind that makes us value the virtues and not want to have delusions in mind, so that we can then engage in positive actions with those virtuous minds, and avoid the non-virtuous actions and deluded minds. Guarding alertness is the mindfulness moral discipline chapter, and it's all about really actively training the mind — how do you train the mind, how do you watch the mind, how do you avoid this action, how do you change that action? It's all about the actions. This is more just the big picture state of mind that values virtue in general and is anti-delusion in general. They're not inherently separate — they're totally mixed together and supporting each other.

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: I was about to ask if it's mindfulness — conscientiousness — but you're saying it's not mindfulness. I'm still confused. You said it's a bigger picture. What exactly is conscientiousness?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Mindfulness just means it's a mind that remembers something and it prevents distraction. That's all mindfulness is. So in modern usage of that word, obviously there's different interpretations, but the way that we use it is specifically like that. It just means a part of the mind that can remember something, hold on to something, and not forget it. That's mindfulness. So you can be mindful of positive things, negative things, neutral things. If you're mindful of a grudge that you have, that's incredibly negative. You keep remembering it over and over and feeling resentful and frustrated. So mindfulness just means a part of the mind that remembers something and prevents us from getting distracted. The practice of being mindful of virtue, guarding the mind — often we'll say that's moral discipline, another way of looking at moral discipline. Guarding the mind with mindfulness and alertness. And the point is, when we're saying it like that, you're really training the mind actively. Conscientiousness is sort of the why behind why you train the mind in the first place.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Let's get an example. Say you want to work out. You can think of conscientiousness as thinking about all the benefits you get from working out and all the problems you get from not taking care of your body. That's going to give you this strong interest in taking care of your physical health — eating right, doing this and doing that. It's sort of this intellectual framework of what's driving you. Where mindfulness of virtue, moral discipline, is like actually working out. You're actually trying to not eat a bunch of garbage. You're actually trying to move your body around. So of course they're related — the reason you take care of your body is because of the intellectual framework, the reasoning. But they're slightly two different things. Some people just start to take care of it but without the why, and then they usually burn out at some point or run out of steam. If you really have the why, powerfully, you stick with it a bit more. Because you understand, I really want to do it. I really get why I do it. I really see the importance and the value. Same with the mind. If we really see the value of virtue, we really see the faults of non-virtue and delusion, then of course we're going to have a much strengthened moral discipline practice. Geshe-la says: conscientiousness should be practiced in conjunction with mindfulness and alertness. So it's like moral discipline is the application of conscientiousness.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Okay. So then, one overarching practice point for all of us. As we come to these classes, we're going to keep diving deeper and deeper and into more subjects and more ideas. And we come to other teachings, we're going to keep going deeper, getting more ideas, more practices. Go to an empowerment, then you get something there. And what I've noticed is that I'm not sure we're all clear about how to do that correctly. So I'm going to take a moment to clarify. For me, I don't have this problem at all. And I think my teachers, when I first started practicing, taught me very well how you exactly do this. And maybe I've done a bad job at teaching how to do this. But I keep hearing enough questions that make it clear to me there's a lack of understanding here. So let's take an example. You have a broth that you're making. You're making a lovely stew. If someone comes up to you and goes, potatoes are so good in stew — have you ever had a potato in your stew? You wouldn't grab your stew, throw it out, grab another pot, start throwing potatoes in. I've got to make potato stew now. You wouldn't forget what you were doing, throw it aside, and just scramble and make something else. And then someone else says, I just had the best cake. You throw your potatoes and your pot against the wall. Let's make cake. It's not like that. It's called catastrophic forgetting. That's the technical name. You're basically lurching. You have something you're building up. Something new comes along. And now you're doing that.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: So in the teachings, there's the lamrim storehouse analogy. It's really helpful. Think of our lamrim practice as a storehouse, like a grocery store or a warehouse. Someone comes along and goes, potatoes are really great. And you're like, that's so cool. Good to know. I got this awesome soup going here. It's not going in the potato direction. But you know what? I got a place to put that potato. Thank you. Potatoes are good. You can make fries and hash browns. They're good in this kind of thing. Cool. And you put it in your storehouse. And you know where it is, and you come back to it when you need it, and you grab it whenever you need to. And then someone says, cake is awesome too. Wow, I love cake. Yeah, I might have a good time for cake. Leave me the recipe. Let's put that one on the shelf too. I know where to put that. I'm working on my stew here. I don't need to jump to cake right now. So in our practice, our daily practice, whatever our main thing that we're working on is like that stew. And it might be the six-session guru yoga. It might be a heart practice with a lamrim meditation. It might be a sutra practice, a little tantric practice. It might be person meditation. It might be just a taking and giving practice. That's the stew. And when we come to a Dharma class, the teacher's job isn't to say, you have a stew, okay, just keep having your stew, I won't tell you anything else about food. The teacher's job is to share the Dharma, and then we have to have the wisdom on how to use that and integrate that and store that where it's supposed to go. So we don't need to lurch from this to that.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: So that's the first point. The second point — and this came up in the tantric course yesterday, so this is why I want to reiterate this more precisely — there's us trying imperfectly. Then there's the optimal way to practice Dharma. We're always just doing our best. And it's going to be imperfect until we're a Buddha. But when we receive Dharma teachings, the teacher still needs to teach us the proper way to do something. But we can't take that as an indictment on our imperfect attempt. It's never a criticism of our imperfect attempt. It's never a judgment on our imperfect attempt. It's also not saying that our imperfect attempt is wrong in isolation. It could be better, of course, but our imperfect attempt is way better than not doing anything. And so we never want to hear that kind of thing through a light of, this is saying I'm bad, or I'm not doing good enough. These are just two different things. We need to know the ideal. We need to keep improving. We can't just stay at the imperfect trying state forever. But we never want to take that as a comment on the fact that we're trying imperfectly. And for me, if I'm worried about people doing that, then what that's going to lead me to do is to never teach people how to actually do things correctly. Which is — we're not really growing anymore then. It's just going to be saying, yeah, good job, we're all doing our best here. And it's comforting to some degree, but in the long run it's not comforting, because we don't break out of anything.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: And then this is the last thing, and it's related to conscientiousness. It's something we've talked about at different times, but it's nice to formalize. In the end of the day, all of Buddhist practice is just about overcoming delusions and increasing our virtues. That's all it boils down to. Getting rid of the delusions and the imprints of delusions, and increasing our virtues. And so in our practice and in our life, having a floor practice — on our worst day, what do we do? Having this formalized and decided is incredibly helpful. And it's really nice to have it related to something around conscientiousness. Something really simple and axiomatic and fundamental. I've talked about the idea of having doing no harm as one of those examples. On my worst day, I'm going to do no harm. I'm going to practice non-harmfulness, which is another name for compassion. Nothing else, but that's what I'm going to do on my worst day. That's my floor. And that's amazing, and that's perfect and beautiful, and we're so in line — we're becoming a Buddha with that decision. But we're also knowing, there's going to be days where we don't have much else, and having too fragile and elaborate of a system that we can't maintain doesn't really work on the worst day. We need something a bit more bedrock-y, rock solid. Or another one is — I'm just going to try to stay with love today and do my best to practice love today. And again, that's the positive side of conscientiousness, the virtue side. I've got not much else going on, but I'm just going to focus on loving people today. And it's not a cop-out — it's a beautiful practice, and it's essential, and it has everything in it. Having a floor practice identified — it is part of our spiritual structure. Having it as a decision that we've made is really nice. And then on those days, we can just feel completely good, encouraged, inspired — I'm doing my floor practice today. It's a floor day. If we have no floor, then what happens is we crash, further, further, further, through a bunch of floors. And then we can really go off the rails. But if we have one that's sturdy enough and virtuous, we bounce back, and we're protected from going too far off the rails.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Okay, so I just wanted to make these three points. I hope they're relevant and useful. They're coming up partially because of some of the questions and points that I heard recently from people, and I wanted to respond. But also because we're in conscientiousness, and it's just this kind of meta mind. It's just saying — virtue, good. Delusion, bad. And it is a great place we can always go back to. It's really the basis of Buddhist faith. Virtue, good. Delusion, bad. That's it. That's kind of Buddhism. Okay, I think that's actually it. I think we'll wrap it up there. We'll return back to some of those bits in conscientiousness. All right. I have a flight at 10, from JFK. So I will dissolve. But we're still going to have discussion. And then maybe Sumit, could you wrangle everyone at 7:20 to identify the meditation break — the meditation object with the purpose, object, and actual meditation identified? Is that okay? Yeah, thank you. Apologies that I'm ducking out. I made a mistake setting the flight for 10 at JFK. That was my bad. But I will learn a lesson.

teaching.text: Discussion-wise — Alexis and Sumit. And Marianne and Jose. And Mimi, Anne, and Ryan. Okay, thank you.
